text: Well done, Chase! You actually ended up at the China Square branch of Ya Kun Kaya Toast. There are countless outlets across the island for Ya Kun Kaya Toast, but the China Square branch is the one said to be still manned by the family/extended family members of the original founders, while all the other outlets are manned by hired staff and franchisees. Taste at this outlet is top notch and consistent! Ah yes, Kaya is a wonderful food to bring back, if your home country allows bringing in for personal consumption. It goes well with most types of assorted breads and crackers! Most visitors would actually get some back for personal consumption. But just remember to keep it in the fridge once opened, till you finish the whole bottle. 👍 Best recommended way to eat the egg would be to mix the pepper and soya sauce well, and slurp it up. And yeah, we usually try not to dip kaya Toast in the coffee, as it will "disintegrate" very quickly. Give you a hack for unusual way of having coffee. We locals and Malaysians call it kopi gao gu you. Or "butter coffee". Simply, just order a cup of coffee like the Ya kun coffee (coffee with condensed milk) and drop a piece of BUTTER in the coffee. Preferably high quality butter like SCS or similar class you can find in your country, then wait for 2 to 3 minutes for the butter to slowly dissolve in the coffee while you sip up that heavenly taste of buttery coffee! Remember not to stir and dissolve the butter completely, as this will spread out the butter flavour all over. You let the butter dissolve naturally and you will have this distinctive taste that taste different with each mouthful. Cheers!

text: A Singaporean food vlogger (Dancing Bacons) called pandan "Asian vanilla" in a recent video. It's pretty horrid by itself, but it just adds so much to whatever it gets put into. I was thinking that gula melaka would have been the sugar used historically. But the flavours in it would have quite an effect on the final taste of your kaya- and not necessarily for the better. You don't mention pandan extract. Fresh is best, but sometimes one must make do with what one can get. It also, from my experience, tends to be coloured a very vivid artificial green. Hot toast and cold butter combine really well. I was told as a kid to eat my crusts otherwise I wouldn't get curly hair. Add this dish of deliciousness to a couple of half-boiled eggs with white pepper and soy sauce. Wash it down with either a kopitiam coffee or a glass of sweet, black Cameron Highlands tea- teh O. This would be on high rotation for breakfast. One day this, the next a roti prata/canai, the next a Western/Singaporean scrambled eggs with turkey sausages and bacon (halal one!), and maybe a combination of what we in Australia call "Singapore noodles" and chicken curry on the fourth day. Fruit, cereal, and yoghurt would be for a brunch.

text: What seems to be missing from the criteria is whether the kaya is actually authentic. One of the featured stores is a good example — it was a bit funny that it got a five-star rating when the camera clearly showed cans of commercial cheap kaya being used. It’d be great to see a bit more attention paid to details like this in future episodes.

text: When I was a kid, I would go 3 doors away to buy double slices of steamed white (or brown sometimes) bread with SCS butter and kaya (made by the coffeeshop). The coffeeshop would roast the coffee seeds spinning manually inside a big drum heated by fire wood, behind the back lane. 9-9.30pm, I would buy the same amount of bread from an elderly Punjabi man, who came on bicycle, carrying a big wooden box behind him. He would also give me some of the toasted slides especially the top layers. These toasted sides gave off a unique aroma when dipped into ovaltine or kopi O. However, bread back then, tasted very much better and they were heavier, than today. Today’s bread mostly are light weighted, don’t taste good and the texture becomes dry on the 2nd day.

text: Even as a local, I love ya kun (though it is pricey for just toast, eggs and coffee) Ya kun is consistent, even 20 years ago to the present day, it's the same product with the same taste tip for foreigners: if you order coffee or tea, it usually comes with condensed milk (so it is sweet) there are some ordering guides online for you to customize your coffee or tea to your taste (search kopi.guide) but some of the more common ones are kopi-o (o means black, no milk) kopi-o-kosong (black coffee + kosong, which means no sugar) kopi-c (c means evaporated milk instead of condensed milk) same thing for the kaya butter toast, if you are cutting calories, you can ask them to not include the butter or swap to a different spread

text: Okay, I love the video and the editing, however, the recipe is awful. Kaya is typically made with whole eggs and cooked for an extremely long time, so this is kind of like a cheat, quick method. This means the results are not the same as real authentic kaya. When I made this today, it was looking great until the very end. The texture was not right, it was more like a thick and gloopy caramel, and the taste was just extremely eggy. I guess that is what you would expect from an easier quicker method, but I was hoping for something way better. As well as that, the recipe only fills up half a jar, not a whole one. Would I recommend this recipe? No, probably not. Only if you are looking for a quick recipe providing eggy and gloopy results. If you really want a proper, authentic kaya taste, this is not the recipe for you.

text: Nice to see your videos around Singapore! Do come here more often, I've been enjoying your videos a lot! A gentle side note, "prata" (the Singapore name) is the localised name for "parotta", the original name of the refined flour, ghee-fried, stretched, layered, flaky bread from Chennai, Tamil Nadu, South India. Not to be confused with "paratha" or "parata", which is basically a non-layered, whole-wheat tortilla-like fried bread with a potato filling, from North India. Very different from "prata". Their dough is very different. Prata is slap-stretched and folded. Paratha, being whole-wheat, is rolled with a rolling pin like stiff bread dough, not unlike tortillas which are pressed. Another fun fact, the Malaysian name for prata is "roti canai" (read as "roti chennai"), which simply means Chennai bread.

text: I’m Singaporean, I can safely tell everyone that’s not based in SG who doesn’t know this, that our eggs are safe to be consumed raw or even when it’s this runny. All our eggs are pasteurised and undergo strict tests to ensure it is safe for our consumption! If they contain salmonella they are rejected and if they have already been released into the market, they will do a public recall of the product with the batch number etc and will ask those that have purchased to return the item as well. Besides that, I’ve eaten soft boiled eggs with kaya/butter toast at toast box/ya kun and at our usual hawker centres but my opinion is that hawkers do it best! Love spamming soya sauce in it, mixing it up and drinking the eggs straight from the bowl, followed by the toast dry or with tea.

text: 1. pandan kaya is not the best pick, XO hainanese kaya is the best for kaya toast 2. bread must be toasted, it can be charred to personal preference but it must be toasted so the butter can melt 3. eggs, soy and pepper needs to be mixed 4. while milo is a choice, coffee or tea is the main go to. Personally, i go coffee + small amount of condensed milk How much to dip to soak the bread in egg is entirely up to preference. some owners use a different type of bread so the amount of egg soaked changes, so dipping however much you want is the way to go but you want the part of toast you biting into to be completely covered Also, a habit i picked up, you want some coffee left before finishing the toast so when you have left overs, you pour the hot coffee and mix with the eggs before drinking it all in a go. Maybe give this a try

text: Kaya 其实没有对不对的颜色。绿色的就是加了斑斓叶。海南式的通常是褐色，娘惹的就是绿色。
text_en: There's no right or wrong colour for kaya. The green one has pandan leaf added. Hainanese style is usually brown; Nyonya style is green.

text: 其實還有一個吃法可以試的就是會把那個蘇打餅稍微泡在飲料（咖啡/鴛鴦/美祿）然後再吃也很讚

text: 拿麵包直接沾著混合了醬油和白胡椒粉的半熟蛋去吃才是人間美味❤❤❤
text_en: Dipping the bread straight into the half-boiled eggs mixed with soy sauce and white pepper is heavenly ❤❤❤

text: 新加坡在地人称它为半熟蛋。 咖椰酱有两种, 绿色的Kaya酱在制作时加入了斑兰叶, 所以呈现绿色及斑兰叶的香气。 褐色的Kaya酱俗称海南咖椰。 一般上两颗蛋的量只需加入半茶匙的黑酱油就可以了, 加太多会死咸。当然如果个人口味重的可以再加一 点, 但吃的太咸对健康不好。
text_en: Singapore locals call it 'half-boiled egg'. There are two kinds of kaya: green kaya has pandan leaves added when made, so it's green with a pandan aroma; brown kaya is commonly called Hainanese kaya. Usually two eggs only need half a teaspoon of dark soy sauce — too much and it's deathly salty. Of course if you like it stronger you can add a bit more, but eating too salty is bad for your health.

text: There are 2 versions of kaya. Green is because pandan juice is added. Whereas for the brown type (hainanese kaya), caramalised sugar is added and pandan leaves are cooked as whole leaves instead of juice. However cheap commercial alternatives, especially the green coloured ones are just made with colouring and flavouring. Ya Kun's bread toast is made extra thin by slicing the bread into half. I personally find it too dry and not much texture for their toast version. Prefer the steamed instead. The soda cream crackers with kaya and butter is what the older generation eat. My father ate this way since he was a kid. Cream crackers with butter and kaya or sugar or jam.

text: 清末，海南島瓊州是最後一個開放海禁。所以，海南人來到馬來亞和新加坡謀生，所有的行業被其他籍貫的人給把持。他們唯有替土生華人和英國人打工，繼承了英國人西餐的一套。一點很多人不知道，Kaya其實源自於葡萄牙，葡萄牙人稱呼為Si Kaya。
text_en: In the late Qing dynasty, Qiongzhou on Hainan Island was the last to lift the sea ban. So when Hainanese came to Malaya and Singapore to make a living, every trade was already held by people of other origins. They could only work for the Peranakans and the British, and inherited the British way of Western cooking. Something many people don't know: kaya actually originates from Portugal; the Portuguese called it 'Si Kaya'.

text: 新加坡平民美食早餐很多；有椰浆饭 （ NASI LEMAK ) ; 印度煎饼 （ ROTI PRATA ) ; 炒米粉； 猪肠粉 （ 米浆制的条状物 ）；炒罗卜糕 ；包点；笋粿；红龟粿；鸡蛋糕；豆浆油条；西式糕点土司等等；丰俭由人。 阿坤的套餐并不是普通新加坡人每天必吃的；抱歉；您只挑一家来介绍；会让广大的网民误会新加坡在地缺乏美食小吃。 您自己有烤面包机的话；早餐就能吃自烤面包；擦上加椰牛油再配一杯黑咖啡；就是一顿神仙早餐咯。 您不妨多尝尝新加坡多元种族不同的平民早餐小吃。
text_en: Singapore has many everyday breakfast foods: nasi lemak, roti prata, fried bee hoon, chee cheong fun (rice-flour rolls), fried carrot cake, steamed buns, soon kueh, ang ku kueh, egg cake, soy milk with youtiao, Western pastries and toast, and so on — something for every budget. Ah Kun's [Ya Kun's] set is not what ordinary Singaporeans must eat every day; sorry, but picking only one shop to introduce will mislead netizens into thinking Singapore lacks local food. If you have a toaster at home, you can toast your own bread, spread kaya and butter and have it with a cup of black coffee — a heavenly breakfast. Do try more of Singapore's multiracial everyday breakfasts.
